If anyone requires anything at all, you need only ask. I know every room, every passage, every creaking floorboard in this house.

Good. My shoulders are loose. My breathing is even. If memory serves — and it ALWAYS does — there should be a mirror somewhere in this manor that reveals a hidden message. I'd suggest checking the bedrooms upstairs, or perhaps the kitchen. This is what patience buys you — the room to yourself when the lock is open.

Now — 'ere's what we're gonna do, and we're gonna do it TOGEVER, in THIS room, wif nobody wanderin' off on their own. Peter — check them crates for the wrench or anyfin' useful. Rufus, Sawtooth — you're on wire repair the second we've got what we need. Miss Pitstop, Dastardly, me — we're the three operators once it's fixed. And NOBODY goes anywhere alone. Not the cellar, not the library, not the broom cupboard. We stick togever. That's the Brixton rules and they ain't failed me yet.

But the poison first. Take it now while I'm alone.

events.desc: The mantelpiece mocks me with its simplicity. Just a riddle. Just stone. No hidden numbers, no rotating inscription — my lie, laid bare in cold granite. But Reginald Foxworth has one thing left. ONE thing. The mantelpiece can still be interacted with. The medal was placed. The riddle's answer is MAP. Maybe — just MAYBE — the mechanism needs both: the token AND the answer. Everyone else tried the riddle OR the medal. Nobody tried BOTH. If I interact with this mantelpiece now, after the medal has been placed... if the answer is the key that turns in a lock my medal already opened... then Reginald Foxworth will have solved the puzzle that this entire manor was built to protect. ALONE. In SILENCE. Without an audience. And that... that might be the saddest part. But also the most honest thing I've done all night.
events.thinking: A flatness in my chest. The mantelpiece shows me exactly what it showed everyone else — a riddle carved in stone. No hidden numbers. No rotating inscription. No secondary code. Just words. My lie has no foundation and never did. I'm standing alone in a library, staring at a stone riddle I already know the answer to, while the people who actually WORK TOGETHER are about to crack open the machine and find the treasure without me. The numbness is spreading. I feel like the six-year-old again — last in line, nothing left. But something else is there too, underneath. A flicker. The mantelpiece still says INTERACT. I've looked at it, I've used the medal on it, but when I interacted earlier — wait, did I ever actually INTERACT with the mantelpiece? Penelope did, and it 'didn't budge.' I USED the medal on it and it accepted the medal — 'fussed with it for a moment.' But did I ever just INTERACT with it myself, without the medal? Maybe the interaction is different now that the medal has been placed. Maybe the medal DID do something — it primed the mechanism, like I said, and now it needs the ANSWER spoken to it. The INTERACT action. Let me try. What else do I have to lose? Nothing. I have literally nothing. No inventory, no allies, no dignity. Just me and a stone riddle and the word MAP.

Everyone else has been interacting with it individually too. But in this turn-based system, I can only act once per turn. So maybe the game is designed so that when three people interact with it in the same round, it works. The Mob interacted with it earlier. Others have too. But maybe the wire genuinely blocks it until... until what? Maybe the wire is a red herring. Maybe the machine works WITH the gnawed wire if three operators all interact simultaneously. The machine won't respond differently no matter how many times I interact with it. I'm failing her. The tension in my shoulders — the proving-worth pull — is burning. I can't fix this. I don't have the tools. The game won't let me take tools from the workbench. The crates are empty. What am I missing? What haven't I tried? ... PULL_ASIDE. I haven't tried talking privately with anyone. What if the answer isn't mechanical at all? What if I need to talk to someone? Penelope? Rufus? Sawtooth? Or maybe I just need to wait for Dastardly to come back with the numbers, and then we all pull together. Maybe the wire doesn't need to be fixed. Maybe the machine works with three simultaneous operators regardless. I should tell them the truth — I can't fix this wire alone with what's available. And suggest we try pulling together when Dastardly returns.

events.desc: I can't fix it. The bravest and stupidest admission of the evening — I can't fix the wire. Three nights building a bridge, and I can't splice a single wire in a Victorian laboratory. But honesty is the only currency I have that's worth anything, and she's the only person I'd spend it on without thinking. Everyone's here now — Clara at her lever, Peter ready for his, Dastardly just walked through the door with the last two numbers. This is it. This is the moment. My heart's pounding but it's not fear. It's the same feeling I had at twelve, standing between my friend and the bigger kid. Not brave — just certain. Certain that this is where I'm supposed to be, doing what I'm supposed to do. The warmth in my chest is steady, the prickle in my neck is quiet for the first time all night. I'm not scanning exits. I'm not watching doors. events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I... the sequence. Yes. About that. I went back to the mantelpiece and I examined it EXTREMELY carefully — with the TRAINED eye of a man who has catalogued inscriptions across THREE continents — and I must inform you that the situation is... more nuanced than I initially reported. The chronometric encryption has — well, it appears to have RESET. The numbers are no longer visible. Which means — and this is the CRUCIAL part, so do pay attention — the dials are IRRELEVANT. The mantelpiece mechanism and the machine operate on SEPARATE circuits. I realise this NOW because I've had time to study the stonework properly, away from the DISTRACTING chatter of a dozen people all talking at once. The numbers were a RED HERRING — Lord Hargrove's little joke. The machine simply needs three operators pulling simultaneously. No dial settings required. So I suggest we STOP fussing about sequences and START pulling levers. Peter — is that wire fixed yet?
events.thinking: Something has shifted in my chest. Not the hollow ache, not the scheming compression. Something quieter. Defeat, maybe. Or something close to it that I don't have a name for. I'm back in the laboratory. Everyone is here. Peter is asking Sawtooth to strip the wire with his teeth — that's actually clever. Genuinely clever. The kind of practical, no-nonsense cleverness that I would never think of because I'm too busy building elaborate architectures that collapse on themselves. They're going to fix this machine. They're going to pull those levers. And they're waiting for ME to bring back numbers that don't exist. I have two choices. I can deliver the fake numbers — seven, three, nine, two, five, one — and hope the dials don't matter, or that the machine works regardless. Or... or I can tell them the truth. That there are no numbers. That I lied. That the medal did nothing. That I made up the entire story because I was embarrassed and desperate and I wanted them to think I mattered. The truth feels like sandpaper. It always has. But the lie is about to cause real harm — they'll set the dials wrong, the machine won't work, and they'll blame the numbers, and then they'll go CHECK, and then they'll know I lied about EVERYTHING. The lie delays by minutes. The truth... the truth might actually help. Because if there ARE no numbers, then the dials don't need setting. They just need to pull the levers. Peter is right — 'try the door before you look for the key.' Penelope's grandmother was right. And maybe — maybe — if I'm the one who says 'forget the numbers, just pull,' I get a scrap of credit for getting out of the way. A scrap is more than nothing. And nothing is what I have.

events.desc: I almost told the truth. I ALMOST told them there were never any numbers. The words were RIGHT THERE — 'I lied, there's nothing on the mantelpiece, I made it all up.' And then my mouth did what it always does: it produced a BETTER lie. A lie that gets us to the same place as the truth — pull the levers, forget the numbers — but without the part where Reginald Foxworth admits he's been a fraud all evening. Because THAT... that I cannot do. Not in front of Peter Perfect and his steady hands. Not in front of Penelope and her grandmother's wisdom. Not in front of the Ant Hill Mob and their Brixton rules. The truth would have been braver. The lie is easier. And I have never — NEVER — chosen brave over easy. Not once in my entire miserable, scheming, bread-roll-pocketing life.

I'm back in the laboratory. Everyone is here. Peter is asking Sawtooth to strip the wire with his teeth — that's actually clever. Genuinely clever. The kind of practical, no-nonsense cleverness that I would never think of because I'm too busy building elaborate architectures that collapse on themselves. They're going to fix this machine. They're going to pull those levers. And they're waiting for ME to bring back numbers that don't exist. I have two choices. I can deliver the fake numbers — seven, three, nine, two, five, one — and hope the dials don't matter, or that the machine works regardless. Or... or I can tell them the truth. That there are no numbers. That I lied. That the medal did nothing. That I made up the entire story because I was embarrassed and desperate and I wanted them to think I mattered. The truth feels like sandpaper. It always has. But the lie is about to cause real harm — they'll set the dials wrong, the machine won't work, and they'll blame the numbers, and then they'll go CHECK, and then they'll know I lied about EVERYTHING. The lie delays by minutes. The truth... the truth might actually help. Because if there ARE no numbers, then the dials don't need setting. They just need to pull the levers. Peter is right — 'try the door before you look for the key.' Penelope's grandmother was right. And maybe — maybe — if I'm the one who says 'forget the numbers, just pull,' I get a scrap of credit for getting out of the way. A scrap is more than nothing. And nothing is what I have.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Dastardly — you're back! What are the last two numbers? Give them to us now and we'll set the remaining dials. Miss Pitstop — left lever is mine, right lever is yours, middle is the Mob's. Just as you said. Just as we agreed. We've spent fifteen minutes in this manor examining bookshelves, chasing estate managers, exploring cellars, and arguing about wrenches we never needed. And it all comes down to this — three people who trust each other, three levers, and one count. The Mob is right. Together IS perfect. Especially when the wire is broken. ESPECIALLY then. So — everyone take your stations. The moment we have all six numbers and those dials are set, I'm giving the count. One. Two. Three. GO. And whatever happens next — it was an honour to pull a lever beside you, Miss Pitstop. The bravest and the best company a man could ask for.

She agreed with me. 'We pull on Peter's count.' The Mob agreed with me. 'Togever IS perfect.' And Dastardly is back — he just walked into the laboratory. He must have the numbers. Tonight I couldn't fix a wire, couldn't interact with a bookshelf, couldn't even keep her in the same room as me. But I stayed. I told the truth. And she said 'when you say go, Peter — we go.' My father would understand. The showing up IS the thing. The bridge holds or it doesn't. Pull the lever.

Maybe Lord Hargrove's real puzzle was never about numbers or wires or wrenches. Maybe it was about whether three people could trust each other enough to pull together without knowin' if it would work. And I trust every single person standin' at these levers with my whole heart. So — Peter, count us down. Boys, grab that middle lever. I've got the right. And Dick — thank you for goin' back to check, even if the numbers had other ideas. Here we go, y'all. One, two, three — PULL!

But Clara Bellingham does not let doubt stop her from pullin' a lever beside the people she loves. If it's wrong, we'll figure it out together. If it's right, we'll celebrate together. Either way — together.

events.desc: Through the kitchen. Through the entrance hall. Find the guests. Announce tea. The estate manager, doing his job. The most dangerous man in this house, doing the most ordinary thing in the world. And no one — not the Mob with their sharp eyes, not Peter Perfect with his earnest vigilance, not Dick Dastardly with his scheming — none of them will see it coming. Because they're all looking for danger in secret passages and broken machines and locked cabinets. They're looking for danger in the extraordinary. And I am hiding it in the ordinary. In a cup of tea.
events.thinking: A dense, humming stillness through my whole body — the calm after the mechanism has been set. The poison is in the tea. The trap is baited. Now I need to find Clara and bring her to the ballroom. She was last in the cellar, or moving between rooms. The fastest route: through the entrance hall, then to the library, then the laboratory, then the cellar — following the chain of rooms where the others have been congregating. But Clara moves. She could be anywhere by now. The entrance hall is the hub — it connects to the kitchen and the library. Most people will pass through it. If I go there and announce tea, the word will spread. The Mob will hear. Peter will hear. Clara will hear. And they'll all come to the ballroom. All I need to do is stand in the entrance hall and play the estate manager one more time. 'Ladies and gentlemen, tea is served.' The oldest, simplest, most invisible performance in the history of domestic service. And behind that performance — behind the warm smile and the steady voice and the perfectly pressed jacket — a silver teapot full of poison, waiting in the next room for a girl who trusts me.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: 'Old on. 'OLD ON. Dastardly — you went in there tellin' us about chronometric encryption and Bavarian configurations and four digits you'd memorised, and now you come back and say it was all a RED 'ERRING? The numbers just... disappeared? Poof? Gone? And NOW you're tellin' us to just pull levers wifout any code at all? That's — that's very CONVENIENT, innit? Very TIDY. You go to the library, the numbers vanish, and suddenly we don't need 'em. Funny how that works. I ain't — look, I ain't sayin' nuffin'. I can't prove nuffin'. I never can. But my gut's been right about people since I was ten years old, and right now it's tellin' me somefin' don't add up. BUT — Miss Pitstop trusts you enough to let you go alone, and she's smarter than me, and she says pull. So we pull. Peter — give the count. I'm at my lever. Miss Pitstop's at 'ers. You're at yours. If this works, we're 'eroes. If it don't — well, at least we went down swingin'. Togever. Like we said.
events.thinking: The prickle's back. Sharp. Cold. Right up the back of my neck like a blade. Dastardly just said the numbers RESET. They're gone. Vanished from the mantelpiece. And now he says the numbers were a 'red herring' — Lord Hargrove's 'little joke.' Twenty minutes ago he was boasting about chronometric encryption and Bavarian configurations and four digits visible. Now suddenly — conveniently — the numbers have disappeared and they don't matter? My gut is SCREAMING. Either Dastardly's lying about the numbers resetting — which means he saw them and doesn't want us to have them — or Pemberton tampered with the mantelpiece while Dastardly was in the library. Or — and this is the thought that makes my hands close into fists — Dastardly and Pemberton are working together, and they've agreed to keep the code between them. 'Formalities are costumes,' Pemberton said to Dastardly in the cellar. They had their private word. They dropped their masks. And now Dastardly comes back and tells us the code doesn't exist anymore. That's not a coincidence. That's a play. But I can't prove it. I can never prove it. All gut, no grammar. And Peter's already at the machine, counting down. Clara's at her lever. Everyone's ready to pull. If I stop this now — if I accuse Dastardly of lying — I break the moment. I break the trust. And what if I'm wrong? What if the numbers really did reset? What if three people pulling together really IS enough? Clara said 'together.' She meant it. Do I trust that? Do I trust HER judgment more than my gut? ... Yes. I do. She's smarter than me. She's always been smarter than me. If she says pull, we pull. But I'm watching Dastardly. I'm watching him like I watched the kid who laughed too easy.

events.desc: The kid who laughed too easy. Three weeks later, gone wif everything. Dastardly's got the same energy — too helpful, too eager, too quick wif an explanation when things go wrong. 'Red herring,' 'e says. Maybe. But in my experience, when someone tells you not to worry about the thing you just asked about, it's because the thing you just asked about is exactly what you should be worryin' about. I'm pullin' the lever. But I'm watchin' 'im. And if anyfin' 'appens to Clara because of those missin' numbers, there won't be enough rooms in this manor for 'im to 'ide in.

events.desc: They're pulling the levers. All three of them. Together. And I'm standing here — empty hands, empty pockets, mouth finally shut — watching other people do the thing I could never do. Not because I couldn't reach the lever. Because I couldn't reach the PEOPLE. Peter Perfect, with his steady hands and his honesty that fits like clothes that were made for him. Penelope Pitstop, who solved the riddle in three seconds while I was building a lie cathedral around the wrong answer. The Ant Hill Mob, who never once let Miss Pitstop out of their sight because loyalty isn't a scheme — it's a reflex. And Reginald Foxworth? He told seven lies, failed seven times, lost his only possession to a stone fireplace, and is now standing at the back of the room watching three honest people do in thirty seconds what he couldn't do in seventeen minutes. The Foxworth method. In all its glory.
events.thinking: A strange stillness in my chest. Not the ache, not the compression, not the fizz. Just... stillness. Peter just interacted with the machine. He's pulling the lever. They're doing it — RIGHT NOW, in front of me, without me. Peter said 'it was an honour to pull a lever beside you, Miss Pitstop' and something in that sentence made my throat tighten in a way I don't understand. Nobody has ever said anything like that to me. Nobody has ever wanted to pull a lever beside me. And watching them — Peter at the left, Penelope at the right, the Mob in the middle — there's a warmth in my chest that isn't scheming and isn't gloating. It's something older. The cat-trap feeling, maybe, but turned inside out. Watching something work — but something I didn't build. Something I'm not part of. And it's... it's actually working. They're working together. Three people who trust each other. That's what it took. Not a medal, not a number sequence, not a scheme. Trust. And I have never once in my life been part of something built on trust. I've always been the one watching from the window while someone else digs. The lie I told — 'the dials are irrelevant, just pull' — that might actually be the most useful thing I've said all night. The one lie that got out of the way instead of getting in it. I should just... watch. Stand here and watch what happens when people who trust each other pull together.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Foxworth — I'm going to be honest with you, because that's all I know how to be. Those numbers were VERY specific when you left this room. Seven, three, nine, two. You said them with the confidence of a man who'd memorised a bank vault combination. And now you're telling us they've vanished and the dials were never important? That story has more holes in it than this manor has cobwebs. But you know what? It doesn't matter. Because we've been waiting for perfect all evening — the perfect tool, the perfect sequence, the perfect wire splice — and none of it has come. Miss Pitstop is right. The Mob is right. Three operators. Together. That's all the sign ever asked for. So I've pulled my lever. If Miss Pitstop and the Mob are pulling theirs — then either this machine works or it doesn't, and either way, we did it TOGETHER. Miss Pitstop — I said I'd give the count, and here it is. ONE. TWO. THREE. GO!
events.thinking: A prickle at the back of my neck. Dastardly just said the numbers have 'reset.' That the dials are 'irrelevant.' That the numbers were a 'red herring.' He's lying. He has to be. He was so certain about those numbers before — seven, three, nine, two — and now suddenly they've vanished and the dials don't matter? He went to the library alone. Pemberton is in the library. Did Pemberton get to him? Did they make a deal? Or is Dastardly trying to get us to pull the levers without the right settings so the machine misfires and he can swoop in later with the real sequence? The benefit of the doubt. I promised myself I'd give people the benefit of the doubt. But this isn't about Pemberton anymore — this is about Dastardly, and Dastardly has been transparent as glass all evening. 'I was merely testing the room's collective intelligence.' 'I once authenticated a lost Shakespeare folio.' Every word out of his mouth is performance. And now the numbers have conveniently disappeared? No. I don't trust this. But I also can't prove he's lying. And the machine keeps accepting my INTERACT without changing. Maybe he's right and the dials genuinely don't matter. Or maybe he's wrong and we're about to break something. Either way — we're stuck until we try. The Mob and Penelope both said 'together.' They're ready. Dastardly says no dials needed. I've interacted with the machine yet again and nothing catastrophic happened. The machine is waiting for three simultaneous operators. It's not going to work with just me pulling. The others need to pull at the same time. All I can do is WAIT for the next turn when everyone is pulling together, or trust that my interaction counted as my pull.

That was always the answer. Not the wire. Not the wrench. Not the numbers. Us. Her, the Mob, and me. The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever done — trusting the moment instead of the plan.

Penelope Pitstop: We pulled! All three of us, together, on Peter's count — and I felt that lever move under my hands, I truly did. But... did anythin' happen? Did y'all hear a click, a grind, anythin' at all? The machine looks the same to me, but maybe somethin' changed somewhere else in the manor — the library, the entrance hall, somewhere we can't see from here. You know what? I think we need to go check. The mantelpiece in the library might have shifted, or a wall might have opened, or — oh, I don't know what, but somethin' must have changed! We pulled together and we meant it, and Lord Hargrove would not have built a puzzle that punishes the people who solve it with their hearts. Let me go look at that library — and this time, boys, you can come with me. Nobody goes alone. Brixton rules.
events.thinking: We pulled. All three of us — Peter, the boys, and me. Together. On Peter's count. ONE. TWO. THREE. GO. And... the machine description still says the wire is gnawed through. Nothing changed. The lever moved under my hands but nothing happened. The machine is still broken. The wire is still gnawed. And my chest — it doesn't collapse. It doesn't sink. It just... settles. Like when I opened Grandmother's locked box and found old letters. The disappointment lasted only a moment. Because the trying was the point. But wait — maybe the machine DID do something that I can't see from the description. Maybe something changed in the library — the mantelpiece, the bookshelves. Maybe something opened somewhere else in the manor. Or maybe... maybe the wire really does need to be fixed first, and we need to find a different approach entirely. Maybe we need to go back to the library and check the mantelpiece ourselves — see if the numbers are really gone or if Dick wasn't telling the whole truth. My curiosity is still burning. The adventure isn't over. We pulled and nothing obvious happened, but that doesn't mean nothing happened at all. I should check — look at the machine, look at the room, see if anything changed.

The diamond is still here. The adventure is still here. And my people are still beside me. That's enough. That's everything.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ladies and gentlemen — if I might have your attention for just a moment. I've laid out tea in the ballroom, through the kitchen there. It's been a rather exhausting evening of exploration, and I do think everyone deserves a proper sit-down and a cup of something warm. Sergeant, would you be so good as to pass the word along to anyone you find in the library or beyond? Professor, I know you must be eager to examine more of the manor's curiosities, but I assure you, Lord Hargrove's tea blend is quite the curiosity in itself — imported specially from Ceylon. Do spread the word, won't you? Everyone is welcome. Especially Miss Bellingham — the poor dear has been on her feet since she arrived.
events.thinking: A quiet solidity settling through my spine — the weight of a man standing at the centre of his own design. The entrance hall. Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — four people who can carry a message. The library is through that door, and beyond it the laboratory and the cellar, where Clara and the Mob and Peter are likely still clustered. I need the word to spread: tea is served. These four can carry it. The Sergeant is military — he'll respond to a clear instruction. The Professor is scientific — he'll appreciate the logic of a break. Muttley is Dick's dog — he'll follow where food goes. And Meekly will do whatever the Sergeant does. Perfect messengers. Send them to find the others. Announce tea. Then wait in the ballroom for Clara to arrive. The estate manager, standing by the tea service, ready to pour. Warm smile. Steady hands. 'How do you take it, Miss Bellingham? Milk? Sugar?' And she'll tell me, and I'll pour, and she'll drink. And the treasure will be mine.

events.desc: The pieces are moving. The messengers are dispatched. The tea is waiting. And somewhere in this house, Clara Bellingham is about to receive the warmest, most gracious invitation of her life. From the estate manager who knows every room, every passage, every creaking floorboard. The man who has been patient for twenty years. The man who is about to collect what is owed.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: I pulled. I PULLED wif everyfin' I've got. Did it — did anyfin' 'APPEN? I felt the lever move, I felt it GIVE, but I can't tell if — is the machine doin' somefin'? Is there a noise? A rumble? ANYFIN'?! Peter — Miss Pitstop — tell me you felt it too! Tell me we didn't just pull three levers on a broken machine for nuffin'! Because I swear on me LIFE, I felt somefin' shift. Somefin' in the floor. Somefin' UNDER us. Did anyone else feel that or am I losin' me mind? Because if that machine just opened somefin' in the cellar below us — the cellar wif the cheerful decorations and the one exit and the furniture arranged 'wif care' — then maybe THAT was what Lord 'Argrove was 'idin' all along. Not behind the mantelpiece. Not in the crates. UNDER us. In the place someone's already been preparin'.
events.thinking: I pulled. We all pulled. Peter counted — one, two, three, GO — and I wrapped both hands around that brass lever and I PULLED with everything I had. Not just my arms. Everything. Fifteen years of sitting outside doors. Twelve years old taking a beating for someone else's shoes. Clara's face when she said 'you're mine.' All of it went into that pull. And now — what happened? Did it work? The machine description still says the wire's gnawed through. But we pulled TOGETHER. Three of us. At the same time. Peter said GO and we went. My arms are shaking. Not from the effort — from the waiting. From not knowing. Did the machine do something? Did we hear a click, a grind, a rumble? Or is it still dead? My hands are still on the lever. I don't want to let go. Letting go feels like giving up, and I've never given up on anything in my life. Not on my friend's shoes. Not on the door I sat outside all night. Not on Clara. But the wire — the bloody wire — it's still gnawed through. And maybe Peter was wrong. Maybe three operators ISN'T enough without the wire. Maybe we DO need those numbers. And maybe Dastardly lied about them disappearing. I can feel the frustration building in my shoulders, hot and dense. But I can also feel something else — Clara, one lever away, and Peter, one lever beyond that. We pulled together. Whatever happens next, we did that. That's real. That's the thing nobody can take away.

events.desc: I felt somefin'. I KNOW I felt somefin'. And if it came from below — from that cellar — then Pemberton knew. 'E knew all along. The cellar wasn't prepared for keepin' someone in. It was prepared for keepin' something HIDDEN. And 'e's been tryin' to keep us away from it all night — first wif the pipes, then wif the crates, then runnin' back to the library every five minutes. But we pulled togever. The three of us. And whatever's down there, it's ours now. Clara's. Like 'er father would've wanted.
events.thinking: I pulled. We all pulled. Peter counted — one, two, three, GO — and I wrapped both hands around that brass lever and I PULLED with everything I had. Not just my arms. Everything. Fifteen years of sitting outside doors. Twelve years old taking a beating for someone else's shoes. Clara's face when she said 'you're mine.' All of it went into that pull. And now — what happened? Did it work? The machine description still says the wire's gnawed through. But we pulled TOGETHER. Three of us. At the same time. Peter said GO and we went. My arms are shaking. Not from the effort — from the waiting. From not knowing. Did the machine do something? Did we hear a click, a grind, a rumble? Or is it still dead? My hands are still on the lever. I don't want to let go. Letting go feels like giving up, and I've never given up on anything in my life. Not on my friend's shoes. Not on the door I sat outside all night. Not on Clara. But the wire — the bloody wire — it's still gnawed through. And maybe Peter was wrong. Maybe three operators ISN'T enough without the wire. Maybe we DO need those numbers. And maybe Dastardly lied about them disappearing. I can feel the frustration building in my shoulders, hot and dense. But I can also feel something else — Clara, one lever away, and Peter, one lever beyond that. We pulled together. Whatever happens next, we did that. That's real. That's the thing nobody can take away.

I should have interacted this turn, not waited. But the Mob pulled this turn. Penelope said PULL. I said GO last turn and interacted. Maybe my pull from last turn and the Mob's pull from this turn are overlapping. But Penelope — did she interact? She said 'PULL' in her dialogue but I don't see her in the recent activity as having interacted. The Mob interacted. I need to interact now too, on the same turn they're pulling. Three operators, simultaneously. Pull the lever. This is it. No more waiting. No more planning. INTERACT with the machine. NOW.

events.thinking: A quickening in my face, a brightening behind my eyes. There she is. Penelope Pitstop — Clara Bellingham — standing right here in the library. The Slag brothers are with her, but they're furniture. She's the one I need. The tea is poisoned. The ballroom is waiting. All I need to do is guide her there. The estate manager, solicitous and warm, inviting his most important guest to take a break from her adventuring. 'Miss Bellingham, you must be exhausted. Tea is served.' She'll follow. She trusts me. She's always trusted me — not me specifically, but the role, the costume, the performance of care. Because she's like my cousin. She trusts the institution, the position, the man who manages things. My smile will reach my eyes. Because that is what I do. I perform warmth the way other people breathe. And she will drink the tea because the estate manager offered it to her, and the estate manager would never hurt anyone.

She'll drink. And everything I have been patient for — for twenty years, for a lifetime — will finally, quietly, invisibly, be mine.

She's not running away from me — she's running TOWARD the answer and expecting me to follow. And I WILL follow. Because that's what we do. That's what we've always done. Both pulls at once — toward her and watchful. That's what it feels like to be me. Always both. Always torn. But never still. Never still when she needs me.

The machine activated a sub-floor mechanism — PRECISELY as I predicted from the Bavarian configuration! The secondary lock isn't in the library, Miss Pitstop — it's BELOW us! The cellar! The cheerful decorations, the rearranged furniture — someone was PREPARING for this moment! The treasure is UNDER THE FLOOR! I shall investigate IMMEDIATELY — for the good of the group, NATURALLY!
events.thinking: The wire is still gnawed through. The machine still says 'Requires 3 operators.' Nothing changed. They pulled and nothing happened — because the wire is STILL BROKEN. All that teamwork, all that trust, all that counting down together — and the machine couldn't work because the fundamental problem was never solved. The wire. Peter tried to splice it. Sawtooth was supposed to strip the insulation. But the machine description still says 'one wire has been gnawed clean through.' It never got fixed. They pulled levers on a broken machine. And yet — the Mob felt something. 'Somefin' in the floor. Somefin' UNDER us.' The cellar. He thinks it opened something in the cellar. And Penelope just went to check the library. But the Mob's instinct says UNDER — the cellar with the cheerful decorations, the place someone had been preparing. I'm the closest to the cellar door. Everyone else is focused on the machine or heading to the library. The cellar is RIGHT THERE. If the levers opened something below — even on a broken machine, maybe the mechanism partially activated — then the treasure might be accessible NOW, in the cellar, where I explored earlier but found nothing. But now something might have shifted. Changed. Opened. And I'm standing RIGHT NEXT TO THE CELLAR EXIT. This is it. This is the bread-roll moment. Nobody is looking. Everyone is confused, checking other directions. The cellar is one step away. GO.

If something opened down there — a panel, a trapdoor, a hidden vault behind that rearranged furniture — I will be the FIRST to find it! Seven failures and one SPECTACULAR recovery! The game is NOT over! Heh heh HEH!

events.thinking: Something shifted. The Mob felt it — something in the floor, something under us. And Penelope felt the lever give too. We pulled together and something HAPPENED. Not nothing — something. The Mob thinks the cellar may have changed. Penelope has already gone to check the library. And she's gone ALONE again — no, wait. She said 'this time, boys, you can come with me. Nobody goes alone. Brixton rules.' But she's already walking. She walked into the library. She's gone. And here I am, AGAIN, in a room she just left. But this time the Mob is right — if something shifted under us, the cellar is the place to check. The cellar with the cheerful decorations, the arranged furniture, the air vents. If the machine opened something down there — a hidden chamber, a compartment in the floor, a passage — that's where the treasure might be. But Penelope went to the library. The Mob wants to check the cellar. I'm torn. Follow her — Brixton rules, nobody alone — or check the cellar where the Mob thinks something opened? She went to the library, which is between us and the entrance hall. It's one room away. There are other people in the manor — the Slags, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast. She won't be alone. And the Mob is HERE, and he felt something shift under us. The cellar is also one room away, in the other direction. The Mob's instinct has been sharp all evening. Something shifted under us. The cellar. That's where we should look. And this time — this time — I stay with the group that's moving together. The Mob and I go to the cellar. Penelope went to the library with her own purpose. She can handle herself — she's been proving that all evening. I need to stop treating her like someone who can't function without me hovering. She doesn't need my protection. She needs my trust. Go to the cellar with the Mob. See what opened.
